# Week 3, Day 3.1 — TypeScript for a shared class

Four concepts. Today you move the login out of every script into one class, and these are what
that class is made of.

> **Every Run starts fresh.** The studio executes your code in a new process each time, so nothing is left over between runs.

| # | Concept | Why today needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `class` | one place to keep the login behaviour |
| 2 | `constructor` and `this` | how the class receives the page it drives |
| 3 | `export` / `import` | how other files reach it |
| 4 | Methods with typed and default parameters | `signIn(user)` that works with or without an argument |

**Expected:** `Hello Leela` then `Bonjour Leela`.

`new Greeter("en")` creates an **instance**. Two instances, same class, different data — which
is exactly how one `LoginPage` class will serve any page you hand it.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 2. `constructor` and `this`

The **constructor** runs once, automatically, when you write `new`. Its job is to set the
instance up.

`this` means *this particular instance*. `this.language` is the field belonging to the object
you're inside, which is what keeps `en` and `fr` from interfering.

**Expected:** two "constructor ran" lines, then `a.count=2  b.count=1`.

Separate instances, separate state. Forget `this.` and you're referring to a local variable that
disappears when the method ends — a silent bug rather than an error.

`readonly` is worth adopting early: it makes "set once in the constructor" a rule the compiler
enforces, which is exactly what you want for locators.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

**Expected:** the two file shapes printed.

**One naming rule that bites people:** a helper file must **not** be called `*.spec.ts`. The
runner collects every `.spec.ts` file and expects tests in it. Name it `login-page.ts` and it's
just a module. The transcript makes this point explicitly — *"dot spec is always executable"*.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 4. Methods with typed and default parameters

`param: string` says what a method accepts. `param = value` gives it a fallback so the caller
can leave it out.

**Expected:** `signing in as leela@gmail.com`, then `katy@gmail.com` twice.

Default parameters are why `await loginPage.signIn()` will read so cleanly today — the common
case needs no argument, and a multi-user test can still pass one.

Every method that touches a browser is `async`, because every browser action returns a Promise.

## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| `class` / `new` | One class, many instances, separate state. |
| `constructor` / `this` | Runs on `new`; `this.x` is *this instance's* `x`. |
| `export` / `import` | Helper files must not be named `*.spec.ts`. |
| `signIn(user = DEFAULT)` | Common case needs no argument. |

**Next:** [Day 3.2 — Your first shared class](/learn/w3/d3/p2)

# Week 3, Day 3.2 — Your first shared class

Login appears in every spec you've written. By the end of this lesson it appears **once**, and
changing it is a one-line edit instead of a search across the suite.

> **Mode: explore.** Write code in the editor and press Run — it drives a real browser and shows you what happened.

## The problem, in numbers

Picture twenty people on a project. Everyone's spec starts with the same four lines: go to the
URL, fill email, fill password, click Login.

Then a developer renames the email field's placeholder.

| | Copy-pasted login | One shared class |
|---|---|---|
| Files to edit | every spec that logs in | **1** |
| Chance of missing one | high | none |
| Time to fix | an afternoon | a minute |

This isn't a Playwright idea, or even a testing idea. It's the reason functions exist. Automation
is supposed to *reduce* effort — a suite that costs an afternoon per rename has given the saving
back.

## Example 1 — the duplication, so the fix has something to beat

**Objective:** write the login inline, twice, and notice what's repeated.

**Expected:** `spec 1 reached: dashboard` and `spec 2 reached: dashboard`.

Count what's duplicated: two placeholders, one button name, one URL pattern — **four pieces of
knowledge about how login works**, now in two places. Multiply by twenty specs.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 2 — the same behaviour, named once

**Objective:** build the class, then use it.

Two rules while you read it: locators are built in the **constructor**, and methods are named
for **what the user does**.

**Expected:** `as Leela -> dashboard` and `as Katy -> dashboard`.

Compare it with Example 1. No placeholders, no button names, no URL patterns — the journey now
reads as a description of what a person did.

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| Locators in the constructor | one edit when markup changes |
| `readonly` | a method can't reassign one by accident |
| `signIn` not `fillAndClick` | the test reads as behaviour, not DOM operations |
| Default parameters | the common case needs no arguments |
| Every method `async` | every browser action returns a Promise |

**Challenge:** add an `openTile(name)` method that clicks a dashboard tile, then use it to open
`Pay Bills`.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## The filename matters

Save this class as `day3-login-page.ts` — **not** `.spec.ts`.

The runner collects every `*.spec.ts` and expects tests inside. A helper named `.spec.ts` gets
collected, contains no tests, and reports as an empty file or an error. As the transcript puts
it: *"dot spec is always executable."*

await browser.close();
console.log("browser closed");
## The real files

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week3/generated/day3-base-page.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `4 passed`.

Two things worth noticing in the spec.

**It uses `beforeEach`, not `beforeAll`.** It takes the `page` fixture, which is a fresh page per
test, so each test signs in for itself. That's the trade from Day 2.2 — full isolation, at the
cost of a login each time. `beforeAll` + `browser` would be faster and coupled.

**The class contains no `expect()`.** It knows how to reach the dashboard; the *test* decides
what should be true there. Day 3.3 explains why that split matters more than it looks.

## Best practices

- **One class per screen**, named for the screen.
- **Locators in the constructor**, `readonly`.
- **Methods named as user actions** — `signIn`, not `clickLoginButton`.
- **Helper files never end in `.spec.ts`.**
- **No assertions in the class.**

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `No tests found` in your helper | it's named `*.spec.ts` | rename to `.ts` |
| `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'goto')` | forgot `this.` | `this.page.goto(...)` |
| Locator is stale after navigation | rebuilt inside a method | build it in the constructor |
| `new LoginPage()` with no page | the constructor needs one | `new LoginPage(page)` |
| Class asserts, so a failure test needs a second method | assertions leaked in | move them to the test |

**Next:** [Day 3.3](/learn/w3/d3/p3) — the distance between this and a real Page Object Model.

parts.title: From shared class to Page Object Model

blocks.text:
# Week 3, Day 3.3 — From shared class to Page Object Model

What you built in [Day 3.2](/learn/w3/d3/p2) *is* the beginning of a Page Object Model. No new API
here — just the four things a production version adds, and why.

## What you already have right

| Already correct | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| One class per screen | a rename touches one file |
| Locators in the constructor, `readonly` | one place to edit, compiler-enforced |
| Methods named as user actions | tests read as behaviour |
| No assertions inside | one method serves success *and* failure tests |

That last one is the rule worth being able to argue. Put `expect(url).toContain("dashboard")`
inside `signIn()` and it can only be used by tests expecting success. The test for a *wrong
password* now needs `signInExpectingFailure()`. Then the locked-account test needs a third.
Three methods, one click.

**The class knows how to ask. The test decides what the answer should be.**

## The four things a real POM adds

| Addition | What it buys |
|---|---|
| A `BasePage` other pages extend | shared plumbing — navigation, waits — written once |
| Components for repeated widgets | a nav bar or table reader isn't a "page" |
| Fixtures that hand pages to tests | no `new LoginPage(page)` in every file |
| Typed test data | `signIn(USERS[1])` instead of two loose strings |

**Expected:** the two shapes printed.

Notice what the fixture version removes: no `new LoginPage(page)`, no `beforeEach` to construct
it. The test declares `{ loginPage }` and receives one ready to use — and a test that doesn't
need it never pays for it.

> This repo has no `framework/` folder yet — it was removed in the August 2026 reset. These are
> shapes being demonstrated, not files you can import. Later weeks build the real thing, and
> `signIn(USERS[1])` above is the same `USERS` you already import from
> `_shared/test-helpers.ts`.

## Where a page object stops

POM is not a place to put everything. It goes wrong in a specific, recognisable way:

| Belongs in the page object | Does **not** |
|---|---|
| locators for that screen | assertions |
| actions a user performs there | test data |
| waiting for that screen to settle | business rules about what *should* happen |
| navigation away from it | other screens' locators |

The failure mode is a `LoginPage` that grows a `verifyDashboardHasThreeAccounts()` method. Now it
knows about the dashboard, it asserts, and two unrelated tests depend on it. Once a page object
starts asserting, it stops being reusable — which was the entire reason for building it.

## What a reviewer checks

- **No `expect()`** anywhere in a page object or component.
- **No test data** hardcoded inside — pass it in.
- **Locators built once**, in the constructor or as fields.
- **No cross-screen knowledge** — one class, one screen.
- **Helper files not named `*.spec.ts`.**
- **Methods named for intent**, so the test reads as a user journey.

**Next:** [Day 3.4](/learn/w3/d3/p4) — your turn.

# Week 3, Day 3.4 — Practice Three problems. No answer key. App: `https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/`. Verified locators: `getByPlaceholder("Enter Email")`, `getByPlaceholder("Enter Password")`, `getByRole("button", { name: "Login" })`, `getByRole("button", { name: "LogOut" })`. Tiles are `

` elements — use `getByText(name, { exact: true })`, and note `"Statements"` matches **two** elements. > Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Day 3.1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) or [Day 3.2](/learn/w3/d3/p2).

## When you're done

**Look at your Problem 3 spec and count the DOM details visible in it.** Ideally zero — no
placeholders, no button names, no CSS. Everything the tests say should be about what a person
did and what should be true afterwards.

That count is the real measure of whether a page object is doing its job. Not how many classes
you have.

## Where this week landed

| Day | Built |
|---|---|
| [Day 1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) | timeouts, the two deadlines, and where settings belong |
| [Day 2](/learn/w3/d2/p1) | isolation, hooks, `page` vs `browser`, dependent tests |
| Day 3 | one shared class, and the road to a Page Object Model |

Three things decide whether automation works, in order: **how well you know the application**,
then the tool, then the language. Everything this week was really about the third — and about
making sure a change in the application costs you one edit rather than twenty.

problems.statement:
**Build.** A `DashboardPage` class, separate from `LoginPage`.

1. Locators for the LogOut button and the `Account Balance` text, built in the constructor
2. `openTile(name)` — clicks a tile by its visible text
3. `currentSection()` — returns the last part of the current URL
4. A test that signs in, opens `Pay Bills`, and asserts the section is `paymentDashboard`

**Where.** A helper `.ts` plus a spec in `week3/generated/`.

**Check yourself.** It passes, and your class contains **no** `expect()`. If you wanted one,
note where — that instinct is what Day 3.3 was about.

> **Hint** — `currentSection()` returning a value the *test* asserts on is the pattern. A method
> that asserts for you would need a variant per expectation.

**Build.** Prove the class earns its keep by surviving a change.

1. Write a spec using your `LoginPage` for all three demo users (Leela, Katy, Jyosthna),
   asserting each reaches `/dashboard`
2. Now **deliberately break it**: change the email locator in the class to
   `getByPlaceholder("Email Address")` — which doesn't exist
3. Run it. Note how many places you had to edit to break it, and how many to fix it

**Check yourself.** Breaking and fixing were each **one line**, and all three tests failed and
then recovered together. Write one sentence stating what the inline version of this would have
cost.

> **Hint** — the demo users are in `USERS` from `_shared/test-helpers.ts`. Don't retype the
> credentials; one of them is easy to get subtly wrong.

**Build.** A two-class setup with a shared base, and a fixture.

1. A `BasePage` holding what both screens need — the `page`, plus a `goto(path)`
2. `LoginPage extends BasePage` and `DashboardPage extends BasePage`
3. A fixture supplying both, so tests write `async ({ loginPage, dashboardPage }) => {}` with no
   `new` and no `beforeEach`
4. Three tests: a successful sign-in, a tile navigation, and a sign-out

**Where.** Helper `.ts` files plus a spec in `week3/generated/`.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No `expect()` in any class**
- **No `new SomePage(...)` inside a test** — the fixture does it
- **No credentials typed in a test** — pass a `USERS` entry
- Every test passes **run on its own**

Then answer in a comment: *which of these three tests would still pass if the login page were
completely redesigned, assuming the placeholders kept their text?*

**Check yourself.** Passes run together, passes run individually, passes with `--workers=4`.

> **Hint** — `test.extend` was shown in Day 3.3. The redesign question is really asking which
> tests depend on *layout* versus on *behaviour*.
